paras: The Nutbush township whipping was an attack in late July 1903 in which about forty masked men beat and whipped a Black man in Nutbush township, apparently in Warren County, North Carolina. The victim had been charged with burning the Kimball stables that spring, but a grand jury had declined to indict him, and he was not expected to recover.

On the night of 29 April 1903, according to a special dispatch from Keats, Virginia, the stables and four horses of W. W. and J. A. Kimball burned, with no clue to the fire's cause and a loss put at one thousand dollars. The coverage does not show whether this was the fire later called "the Kimball stables" in the whipping report. The man later attacked had been charged with burning the Kimball stables, but the grand jury at the June term of court "failed to find a true bill."

On a Thursday night, described as "of last week" in the local Warren Record and probably about 23 July, about forty masked men "terribly beat and whipped" the man in Nutbush township. His name was not given.

"From the last report," the Warren Record wrote, "it was hardly thought that the negro could recover." No later report of his recovery or death, of arrests, or of any official inquiry appears in the coverage.

The only known account is a short item from the Warren Record, reprinted on the front page of the Raleigh News & Observer on 1 August 1903 under the headline "MASKED MEN BEAT A NEGRO." The item recorded the failed indictment alongside the beating without comment on the masked band or any call to find its members. No Black-press coverage of the attack was found, and no other white paper was found to have carried it.
